extracted.intended_audience: readers of Charles Lamb's letters; students and general readers of 19th-century English literature
extracted.subtask_description: Interpreting and assessing Charles Lamb's personal letters (1815–1819), which include remarks on poetry, humor, lectures, theatrical adaptation, printing, and taste. Useful for extracting Lamb's implicit standards for literary and performative quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: “The humor, if it is meant for humor, is forced;” (critique of a mock 'Peter Bell').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour should arise naturally from matter and manner rather than feel contrived or laboured. Forced attempts at levity harm the piece's effect; the writer prefers humour that feels effortless and organic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of manner to matter
rubrics_metrics.description: “'Hart-leap Well' is the tale for me; in matter as good as this, in manner infinitely before it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work's manner (style, treatment) must suit and ideally elevate its matter (subject). Even with equally good subject-matter, superior manner can make one piece preferable to another. Evaluate both components separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directness of address / narrative mode
rubrics_metrics.description: “The auditors, to whom it is feigned to be told, do not arride me. I had rather it had been told me, the reader, at once.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A narrative pretending to an in‑story audience (auditors) can distance or frustrate the actual reader. Direct address to the reader may be more satisfying; choose narrative stance to maximize reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style must suit the work (avoid over-lyricism)
rubrics_metrics.description: “I cannot say the style of it quite satisfies me. It is too lyrical.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overly lyrical or ornate style can be inappropriate for certain pieces. Match tone and diction to the intended effect; excess lyricism may obscure clarity or undermine humour/irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading and textual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: “One blunder I saw and shuddered at. The hallucinating rascal had printed 'battered' for 'battened'... The Reader (as they call 'em) had discovered it, and given it the marginal brand; but the substitutory 'n' had not yet appeared. I accompanied his notice with a most pathetic address to the printer not to neglect the correction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typographical errors and misprints can distort meaning and disturb readers; careful proofreading and prompt correction by printers/editors is essential to preserve authorial intent and avoid jarring blunders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of medium/format for visionary material
rubrics_metrics.description: “Never tell thy dreams,' and I am almost afraid that 'Kubla Khan' is an owl that won't bear daylight. I fear lest it should be discovered, by the lantern of typography and clear reducting to letters, no better than nonsense or no sense.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some visionary, fragmentary, or intensely imagistic material may lose power when rigidly transcribed or over-explained. Consider whether certain pieces are better left oral, fragmentary, or presented with caution to avoid demystifying them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery mode affects public lectures/performances
rubrics_metrics.description: “If read, they are dismal flat, and you can't think why you are brought together to hear a man read his works, which you could read so much better at leisure yourself; if delivered extempore, I am always in pain lest the gift of utterance should suddenly fail the orator ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manner of delivery (reading vs extempore) crucially alters audience reception: reading can be flat and disengaging, while extempore delivery brings life but carries risk of failure. Speakers should choose a mode that balances clarity, engagement, and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical adaptability for the stage
rubrics_metrics.description: “Coleridge has sent his tragedy to D.L.T.; it cannot be acted this season, and by their manner of receiving I hope he will be able to alter it to make them accept it for next.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic works must account for practical staging constraints (casting, season, managerial taste). Playwrights should be prepared to revise to suit the theatre's practicalities to secure production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and imitation should be identifiable and not merely malicious
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary on a spurious/mock 'Peter Bell' in shops: 'Is there no law against these rascals? I would have this Lambert Simnel whipped at the cart's tail.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parodies or imitative pieces that too closely mimic originals (or are deceptive) confuse readers and may be perceived as malicious or dishonest. Satire/parody should be clearly signaled or crafted so as to avoid unfairly misrepresenting its target; legal/ethical considerations apply to spurious publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical discrimination is a necessary faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: “To G.D. a poem is a poem ... I do not think he has the most distant guess of the possibility of one poem being better than another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and critics should cultivate the ability to discriminate between works of varying quality. A lack of taste or discrimination undermines meaningful literary judgment and the value of critical exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and physical presentation of books matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Remarks on binding/chaining books to shelves and on distribution of presentation copies: 'I will bind up the
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How books are presented (binding, inclusion in a collection, physical handling) and editorial selection (which pieces to include) affect readership and reception. Editors and authors should consider arrangement, selection, and physical form to respect readers' use and signal value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader behaviour and social signaling
rubrics_metrics.description: “Some borrow to leave you an opinion of their sagacity... some neither read nor meant to read, but borrow to leave you an opinion of their sagacity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that borrowing/reading practices are sometimes social signals rather than sincere engagement. Authors and editors cannot assume all circulation equals readership; mechanisms (e.g., presentation, binding) influence actual use.
